results.evidence: I ran the real CLI against a migrated database in $TMPDIR, with stdin from /dev/null. I logged a lead with --phone '(801) 555-0134', received 2026-11-10 09:00. That succeeded as lead 5 (rc=0). I then logged --phone '801.555.0134' with no email, received 2026-11-10 15:00, the same Denver date. It printed 'warning: possible duplicate of lead(s) 5 received 2026-11-10' and 'refused: duplicate not confirmed (use --confirm-duplicate)', exited 1, and saved nothing (leads count stayed 5). Rerunning with --confirm-duplicate printed the same warning and then saved lead 6 (rc=0). The check is find_same_day_duplicates in cottonwood/inbound.py. It matches on email_norm OR phone_e164 and compares local dates. cottonwood/cli.py refuses when the duplicate list is non-empty and _duplicate_confirmed returns False. That function returns False without a terminal. I did not run the repo's test file tests/test_inbound_duplicates.py. One oddity: the database file had been used before my run, so the first lead got id 5 rather than 1. I did not look into why. It does not affect the result.

I ran this against a migrated scratch DB in $TMPDIR. Lead 2 (email A@x.com, phone 303-555-0101, 2026-03-10 09:00) was logged with rc=0. A second inquiry with the same email and no --confirm-duplicate was refused with rc=1 and no lead was created. The same inquiry with --confirm-duplicate exited 0 and created lead 3, whose inquiry_logged payload has duplicate_of [2]. A third inquiry (phone channel, same normalized email and phone, --confirm-duplicate) exited 0 and created lead 4 with duplicate_of [2, 3]. That is the full list of matching ids, so the multi-match case works. The DB also held unrelated earlier rows (leads 1, 5 and 6, from an earlier command in this session that may have partly run), which don't affect this result. The code path is cli.py `find_same_day_duplicates` followed by `log_inquiry(..., duplicate_of=duplicates)`, and inbound.py writes the ids into the payload.

In _duplicate_confirmed, when stdin is a tty it calls input('Save anyway? [y/N] ') and returns answer.strip().lower() in ('y','yes'). So 'y' and 'YES' return True and the inquiry is saved. 'n' and '' return False, and _run_log_inbound then returns EXIT_REFUSED (1) before inbound.log_inquiry is called, so nothing is written. tests/test_inbound_duplicates.py monkeypatches sys.stdin.isatty to True and builtins.input. test_tty_yes_saves (lines 101-116) covers 'y', 'YES' and ' yes ', asserts EXIT_OK and that the lead count is 2. test_tty_other_answers_refuse (lines 119-127) covers 'n', '' and 'maybe', asserts EXIT_REFUSED and that the table counts are unchanged. I ran the test file: 14 passed. I did not get a real pseudo-terminal run: the sandbox refused my pty script as too complex, so this rests on the code and the monkeypatched tests.

I ran the commands against a fresh migrated DB in $TMPDIR with stdin from /dev/null. All four saves exited 0 and printed no warning on stderr. (1) a@example.com received 2026-11-16 23:30 local saved as lead 1. (2) The same email at 2026-11-17 00:30 local saved as lead 2 with rc=0 and no warning. The two inquiries share a UTC date but fall on different Denver dates, and find_same_day_duplicates compares timeutil.local_date values. (3) b@example.com with phone 303-555-0142 on 2026-11-17 saved as lead 3 with rc=0. (4) c@example.com with phone 303-555-0199 on 2026-11-17 saved as lead 4 with rc=0, so a non-matching email and phone on the same day also save cleanly.
